messages.subject: Data cleaning best practices
parts:
I am expecting that this is a very basic question, but I want to ensure I am using best practices, am consistent across animals and have a way to reference why/why not points are being considered outliers. I may be overthinking, but might get some scrutiny here. 

I am planning to use an error model with the data that I am analyzing, but it would be good to understand both paths (error model/no error model available).  Would you mind stepping through your high-level process for determining outliers and cleaning data prior to analysis?

Here is where I am headed, but before I get going, I want to be sure it is the right path (see questions inline):
  1. I am using Movebank, so I would think I remove the null points and any obvious outliers (based on impossible visual locations) there, then pull the data into R.
  2. Is the correct approach to then use amt or move packages (are these best packages to do this?) to remove: 
    1. points where the timestamp is less than 1 minute apart (Do I always assume these points are in error? My fix schedules are 6 pts/hr and 1 pt/hr);
    2. 2D fixes (do I always assume these points are in error?, maybe I should just remove these in Movebank?);
    3. GPS fixes where the speed or distance traveled is improbable. 
  3. Finally, since I am using calibration data with an error model, I should leave all fixes regardless of HDOP values. If I have no calibration data, I would assume UERE = 10 and still leave high HDOP?
  4. Any other steps ...

I want to do roughly the same process for each animal, have a rationale and be able to explain it. Many thanks!

messages.subject: Re: Data cleaning best practices
parts:
I found a good resource for thinking about outliers in general and have answered some of my own questions. I am a newbie, so sorry for the basic stuff.

Here's the path I am taking:
1. For the tracking data, I am removing fixes that are duplicate, null, 2D, obviously bad based on visual inspection, and less than 5 minutes apart.
2. I am thinking I should do the same for my calibration data.

I am then rechecking both files for improbable speed or distance outliers.  After this is complete, I'll fit an error model to my calibration data and then use that with the tracking data.

I guess my outstanding question now (among the million others that keep coming up) is how intensively I should be removing what appear to be outliers from my calibration data.  In other words, I know the unit was in the same spot, so am thinking I should be removing points that look visually distant from that spot.  Is that right or do I leave these points for the model? Ugh ...

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Data cleaning best practices
parts:
Hi Vickie,

Sorry for the delay, I had to have my appendix removed.

  1.  Obvious outliers are generally good to remove, unless they have an appropriately large DOP values and you are sparse on data.
  2. I'm not sure where 'amt' fits in here, but I'm not super familiar with the package.
  3. When you have outliers, its a good idea to figure out if there is some proxy/covariate associated with them when DOP value doesn't (DOP value is supposed to). I do this by importing the data with keep=TRUE, running uere.fit, uere<-, residuals, and then plotting the square residuals against different columns/covariates. I've seen cases where 3D/2D fixes needed to be broken into two different location classes, because otherwise the 2D fixes looked like outliers (DOP value is supposed to account for this). I've seen cases where timed-out fixes needed to be broken into two different location classes, because otherwise the timed-out fixes looked like outliers (again, DOP value is supposed to account for this). The only thing I recall about your data from AniMove was that you had outliers corresponding with location fixes that were at higher than programed sampling rates (2 minutes versus 1 hour or something). If you can figure out something that gives a larger variance in the errors, then you can either introduce a new location class and try to model that variance or filter out those locations. You might use the reduced Z^2 statistic to guide that decision.
  4. Yes, that's what the outlie function is for.
Best,
Chris
